x: Under Article 87 the President addresses the first session after each general election and the first session of each year.

s: For how long does a President elected to fill a vacancy caused by death or resignation hold office?
o: A full term of five years
Until the next Lok Sabha election
x: A President elected to fill a vacancy gets a full five-year term, not the unexpired part of the predecessor's term.

s: Who presides over the Rajya Sabha while the Vice-President acts as President under Article 65?
o: Senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha
x: The Vice-President stops functioning as Chairman while acting as President, and the Deputy Chairman presides.

s: After President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office, who acted as President?
x: Vice-President B.D. Jatti acted as President after Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office.

s: Within what period must an election be held to fill a vacancy in the office of President caused by death or resignation?
x: Article 62(2) requires the election within six months of the vacancy.

s: Who acts as President when the offices of both the President and the Vice-President are vacant?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
x: Under the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969, the CJI acts, and then the senior-most Supreme Court judge.

s: Who was the only Chief Justice of India to act as President?
x: CJI M. Hidayatullah acted as President from 20 July to 24 August 1969.

s: On what does the President's appointment of the majority party leader as Prime Minister rest?
x: Appointing the majority leader as PM is a convention; Article 78 is the separate right to seek information from the PM.

s: What is the position under Article 74(2) of the advice tendered by Ministers to the President?
o: Cannot be inquired into by any court
Can be inquired into by the Supreme Court only
Can be inquired into by a High Court
x: Article 74(2) says whether and what advice was tendered cannot be inquired into by any court.

s: Which of the following does the President do on ministerial advice rather than as situational discretion?
o: Appointing a PM in a hung Parliament
Dismissing a government that has lost its majority
Dissolving the Lok Sabha in special situations
x: Ambassadors are appointed on ministerial advice; the other three are situations of limited discretion.

s: Who is the real or de facto executive in India?
o: Prime Minister heading the Council of Ministers
x: The President is the nominal (de jure) executive; the PM with the Council of Ministers is the real (de facto) executive.

s: What must the President do after returning the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration?
o: Refer it to the Supreme Court
x: The 42nd Amendment made advice binding; the 44th allows one return, after which the President must act according to the advice.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding on the President?
x: The 42nd Amendment made the advice binding; the 44th later allowed the President to return it once.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 65 — Vice-President to act as President
Article 72 — Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
x: Article 65 provides for the Vice-President acting as President in specified circumstances. Article 72 concerns pardon, Article 74 concerns aid and advice by the Council of Ministers, and Article 76 concerns the Attorney General.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Article 60 deals with the President's eligibility for re-election
Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President
Article 56 deals with the President's term and resignation to the Vice-President
Article 58 lays down the qualifications for election as President
x: Article 60 concerns the President's oath or affirmation; eligibility for re-election is in Article 57.

s: Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation as Vice-President in July 2025 and the subsequent election of C. P. Radhakrishnan are relevant primarily to which constitutional provisions?
x: Articles 65 and 68 deal respectively with the Vice-President acting as President and the filling of a vacancy in the office of Vice-President. The July 2025 resignation therefore invoked these provisions.

s:
Assertion (A): The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
Reason (R): Article 64 assigns this role to the Vice-President.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 64 is the provision that makes the Vice-President ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

s: Which Article contains the 15% size limit on the Council of Ministers?
x: Article 75(1A) sets the size limit; Article 74 is aid and advice, 75(3) collective responsibility and 76 the Attorney-General.

s: Which Article vests the executive power of the Union in the President?
x: Article 53 vests the executive power; Article 52 creates the office and 54 sets the electoral college.

s: Which Article makes it the Prime Minister's duty to keep the President informed?
x: Article 78 is the PM's duty to inform; 77 is conduct of business, 76 the Attorney-General.

s: Which Amendment added the 15% size limit on the Council of Ministers in Article 75(1A)?
x: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A) capping the Council of Ministers at 15%.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 66 – There shall be a Vice-President
Article 67 – Vice-President to act as President
Article 65 – Vice-President to act as President
x: Article 65 covers the Vice-President acting as President; Article 63 creates the office, 66 covers the election and 67 the term and removal.

s: What do Articles 52 to 78 of the Constitution of India constitute?
o: Part V, Chapter I dealing with the Union Executive
Part VI, Chapter I dealing with the State Executive
Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights
Part V, Chapter II dealing with Parliament
x: Articles 52 to 78 fall under Part V, Chapter I, which deals with the Union Executive.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Elected members of the Lok Sabha – Vote in both the Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections
Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha – Vote in the Vice-Presidential but not the Presidential election
Members of State Legislative Councils – Vote in the Presidential election
Elected members of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies – Added to the Presidential Electoral College by the 70th Amendment
x: Members of State Legislative Councils vote in neither the Presidential nor the Vice-Presidential election.

s: The Eleventh Constitutional Amendment of 1961 is associated with which of the following changes?
o: Removal of nominated members from the Vice-Presidential electoral college
Providing for election of the Vice-President by State Legislatures
Ending the joint-meeting method for the election of the Vice-President
Introduction of direct election to the office of Vice-President
x: The Eleventh Amendment ended the earlier joint-meeting method and provided for election of the Vice-President by the members of both Houses of Parliament.

s: Which of the following constitutes the electoral college for the election of the Vice-President?
o: All MPs and the State Legislative Assemblies
All members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated
x: All MPs, elected and nominated, vote by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and secret ballot; State Assemblies do not take part.

s: A candidate for Vice-President must be qualified for election as a member of which House?
x: A Vice-President must be qualified for the Rajya Sabha, besides being an Indian citizen aged 35 holding no office of profit.

s: The electoral college for the 16th Vice-Presidential election (2022) had how many members?
x: The 16th VP election (2022) had an electoral college of 788 members, all MPs.

s: To whom does the Vice-President address his resignation?
x: The Vice-President resigns to the President; the President resigns to the Vice-President.

s: How is the Vice-President removed?
o: A Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha
An order of the Supreme Court
x: The VP is removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha; impeachment applies only to the President.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Vice-President?
o: Nominated MPs vote in his election
Elected MLAs vote in his election
He is not a part of Parliament
There is no six-month deadline to fill his vacancy
x: No MLAs vote for the Vice-President; his electoral college is all MPs, elected and nominated.

s: A candidate for Vice-President needs how many proposers and seconders?
x: A VP candidate needs 20 + 20; a Presidential candidate needs 50 + 50.

s: President Droupadi Murmu promulgated the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026. What change did the Ordinance provide?
o: Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 37 to 40, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, including the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 31 to 33, excluding the CJI
x: The 2026 Ordinance increased the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, with the Chief Justice of India excluded from this count.

s: An ordinance promulgated by the President lapses how long after Parliament reassembles?
x: An ordinance must be laid before Parliament and lapses six weeks after reassembly unless approved.

s: In which case was repeated re-promulgation of ordinances in Bihar held a fraud on the Constitution?
x: D.C. Wadhwa (1987) held routine re-promulgation in Bihar a fraud on the Constitution.

s: How many judges decided Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), which held that laying an ordinance is mandatory?
x: Seven judges decided Krishna Kumar Singh (5:2): laying is mandatory and the satisfaction is reviewable.

s:
Consider the following statements about the ordinance-making power:
1. The President may withdraw an ordinance at any time.
2. An ordinance is not subject to judicial review.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1 is correct: an ordinance may be withdrawn any time, and it is subject to judicial review.

s: In respect of which Bills is the suspensive veto of the President NOT available?
x: A suspensive veto returns an Ordinary Bill once for reconsideration, with assent mandatory if passed again; it does not apply to Money Bills.

s: What time limit does the Constitution fix for the President to decide on an Ordinary Bill?
x: Article 111 prescribes no time limit, which is why the pocket veto works in India.

s: In respect of which of the following must the President give assent, so that the absolute veto cannot apply?
o: A Government Bill when the Cabinet resigned before assent
x: A Constitutional Amendment Bill must receive assent; absolute veto may apply to a private member's Bill or a Government Bill after the Cabinet resigns.

s: Which veto does the President of India NOT possess?
x: The qualified veto (overridable by a higher majority) is a US feature; the Indian President has the other three.

s: Who can grant a pardon in a court-martial case?
o: Both the President and the Governor
Neither the President nor the Governor
x: Only the President can pardon a court-martial sentence; the Governor has no such power.

s: Under Article 72, the President's power of pardon does NOT necessarily cover which of the following?
o: Sentences imposed under State laws, in every case
Offences against laws within the Union's executive power
All cases involving a death sentence
x: Article 72 covers court-martial sentences, Union-law offences and all death sentences, but not sentences under State laws in every case.

s: Which form of executive pardon may substitute a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment?
x: Commutation replaces a punishment with a lighter one, such as a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment. Remission only shortens the term.

s: The pardoning powers of the President under Article 72 and of the Governor under Article 161 relate mainly to offences against which laws, respectively?
x: The President deals with offences against Union laws, while the Governor deals with offences against State laws.

s: What does a reprieve mean?
o: A temporary stay of execution of a sentence
Removal of both sentence and conviction
Substitution of a lighter form of punishment
Reduction of the period without changing its character
x: A reprieve only postpones execution temporarily; removal of sentence and conviction is a pardon.

s: Which pardoning power awards a lesser sentence because of special personal circumstances such as pregnancy or physical disability?
x: A respite gives a lesser sentence because of special circumstances such as pregnancy or disability. Remission shortens a sentence without changing its nature.

s: Which form of pardoning power removes both the sentence and the conviction?
x: A pardon removes both sentence and conviction; a reprieve only postpones execution.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cases on the pardoning power?
o: Maru Ram (1980) held that the power is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers
Kehar Singh (1989) held that the President may examine the evidence afresh
Epuru Sudhakar (2006) allowed limited judicial review on mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds
Kehar Singh held that a convict has a right to an oral hearing before the President
x: Kehar Singh held that the President may examine evidence afresh but the convict has no right to an oral hearing.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold in Kehar Singh (1989) about a mercy petitioner before the President?
o: Has no right of oral hearing
Has a right of oral hearing
Must be heard by the Supreme Court first
x: Kehar Singh held the President may examine evidence afresh but there is no right of oral hearing.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The President can pardon a death sentence.
2. The Governor can pardon a sentence passed by a court-martial.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only the President can pardon a death sentence or a court-martial sentence; the Governor cannot.

s: What is the nature of the pardoning power of the President under Article 72?
o: An executive power exercised in his discretion
A judicial power exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice
A legislative power of the Executive
A power exercised on the Supreme Court's advice
x: Article 72 is a judicial power of the President, exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice.

s: Which form of pardoning power reduces a sentence of two years' rigorous imprisonment to one year's rigorous imprisonment?
x: Remission shortens the period without changing the character; commutation changes the form.

s: Which form of pardoning power substitutes a lighter form of punishment?
x: Commutation changes the form (death to rigorous life imprisonment); remission only reduces the period.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Pardon – Removes both sentence and conviction
x: Respite is a lesser sentence for special reasons like pregnancy or disability; a temporary stay of execution is a reprieve.

s:
Consider the following statements about the pardoning power under Article 72:
1. Article 72 covers sentences by court-martial.
2. Amnesty falls within Article 72.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1 is correct: Article 72 covers court-martial, Union-law offences and death sentences; amnesty is outside it.

s: On which Bill did Dr. Rajendra Prasad exercise the absolute veto?
x: Rajendra Prasad used the absolute veto on the PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954, on the Council of Ministers' advice.

s: Which Bill did President Giani Zail Singh keep pending by using the pocket veto?
x: Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986, the only use at the Union level.

s: The ordinance-making power of the President under Article 123 is regarded as a relic of which earlier enactment?
x: The President's ordinance-making power under Article 123 is a relic of the Government of India Act, 1935, which gave the Governor-General power to issue ordinances. The 1909 Act brought Morley-Minto reforms, the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy, and the 1947 Act ended British rule; none is the stated source of Article 123.

s: When can an ordinance be promulgated?
o: a Proclamation of Emergency is in force
the Lok Sabha passes a resolution permitting it
both Houses are in full session
x: An ordinance can be issued only when the legislature is in recess and the Head of State is satisfied that immediate action is needed; none can be issued while both Houses are sitting.

s: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limitations as which of the following?
o: An Act of Parliament or State Legislature
A judicial decree of the Supreme Court
An executive or administrative order only
x: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limits as an Act of Parliament or the State Legislature. It is legislative, not executive, and cannot amend the Constitution.

s: Under which Article is an ordinance treated as 'law', so that it is void if it abridges Fundamental Rights?
x: An ordinance is 'law' under Article 13(2) and is void if it abridges Fundamental Rights, though it can make or change tax provisions within legislative power.

s: Which of the following can an ordinance NOT do?
x: Within legislative competence an ordinance can amend Acts, act retrospectively and change taxes, but it cannot amend the Constitution.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ordinances?
o: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
The ordinance-making power is beyond judicial review.
Re-promulgation without legislative ratification may subvert the Constitution.
The Governor can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
x: Ordinances are subject to judicial review; the other three statements are correct.

s: When can the President withdraw an ordinance?
o: Only within six weeks of reassembly
x: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time; saying he cannot is a common trap.

s: Which Article fixes the maximum gap of six months between two sessions of Parliament?
x: Article 85 sets the six-month limit for Parliament; Article 174 does the same for State Legislatures.

s: If the two Houses reassemble on different dates, from which date is the six-week life of an ordinance counted?
o: the earlier of the two dates
the date the Rajya Sabha reassembles
the later of the two dates
x: An ordinance must be laid before the legislature on reassembly, and if the Houses meet on different dates the six weeks run from the later date.

s: After what period of unexcused absence may an MP's seat be vacated under Article 101(4)?
x: Unexcused absence for 60 days can vacate the seat; prorogation and adjournments of more than four consecutive days are left out of the count.

s: What is the maximum life of an ordinance?
x: The gap between sessions can be six months, and the ordinance lapses six weeks after reassembly.

s:
Consider the following statements about an ordinance issued by the President:
1. It ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved.
2. It ceases earlier if both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: An ordinance lapses six weeks after reassembly, and ends earlier if both Houses disapprove it or it is withdrawn.

s: In which of the following cases does an ordinance end before six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament?
o: When the Supreme Court is in vacation
When both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it
When the Lok Sabha Speaker objects
x: Disapproval by resolutions of both Houses, or withdrawal by the President, ends an ordinance earlier.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)?
o: Every Ordinance automatically becomes a constitutional amendment
Routine re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution
The President’s satisfaction is never subject to review
An Ordinance must remain in force for at least six months
x: D.C. Wadhwa held that routine re-promulgation without placing the Ordinance before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution.

s: In which case (2017) did the Supreme Court hold that re-promulgation of an Ordinance may be a fraud on the Constitution?
o: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
A.K. Roy v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
x: Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that re-promulgation can be a fraud on the Constitution and that laying the Ordinance before the legislature is mandatory.

s: Which recent development revived the debate on the possible misuse of the ordinance-making power and executive overreach?
o: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
The Inter-State Water Disputes Amendment Ordinance, 2026
x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.

s: What is the principal criticism of the frequent promulgation of ordinances?
o: They can be issued only during a financial emergency.
They require prior approval from the Supreme Court.
They transfer all legislative powers to the States.
x: Frequent ordinances are criticised because they bypass parliamentary deliberation.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Article 368 – amendment power not available through an ordinance
Article 13(2) – an ordinance abridging Part III rights is void
x: The Krishna Kumar Singh case was decided in 2017; 1987 is the D.C. Wadhwa case, which condemned repeated re-promulgation in Bihar.

s: Under which Article did Andhra Pradesh use an ordinance on organ-transplant committees?
x: The Governor's ordinance power is Article 213; AP used it for organ-transplant committees.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment made the President’s satisfaction in promulgating an Ordinance final, and which Amendment reversed that position?
o: 38th Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
39th Amendment made it final; 42nd Amendment reversed it
42nd Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
44th Amendment made it final; 38th Amendment reversed it
x: The 38th Amendment of 1975 made the President’s satisfaction final, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.

s: Which Article provides for the Governor's pardoning power?
x: Article 161 gives the Governor pardoning power for offences against State laws.

s: In respect of a death sentence, which of the following can the Governor NOT do?
x: The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence but can suspend, remit or commute it; only the President can pardon it.

s: In which case was limited judicial review of pardons on mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds laid down?
o: Epuru Sudhakar v Govt of AP (2006)
x: Epuru Sudhakar (2006), an AP case, allows limited judicial review of pardons.

s: How did the Supreme Court in Maru Ram (1980) hold that the pardoning power is exercised?
o: On the Council of Ministers' advice
On the advice of the Supreme Court
On the advice of the Home Secretary
x: Maru Ram held the power is exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the pocket veto of the President of India?
o: As in the USA, the President must decide within 10 days, failing which the Bill becomes law.
It is possible because Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the President's decision on a Bill.
Under it, the President neither assents to, nor rejects, nor returns the Bill.
President Giani Zail Singh used it on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
x: The 10-day limit is a US feature; Article 111 sets no time limit in India, which is what makes the pocket veto possible.

s: To which Bills does the suspensive veto of the President apply?
x: The suspensive veto (return once) applies only to Ordinary Bills, not Money Bills.

s: To which Bills is the absolute veto of the President usually applied?
x: The absolute veto is used for private members' Bills and for Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent.

s: Where is the rule that a Bill becomes law if not decided within 10 days found?
x: The 10-day rule is a US feature; Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the Indian President.

s: What can the President do with a Money Bill passed by Parliament?
o: Assent or withhold assent, but not return it
Keep it pending only for ten days
x: For a Money Bill the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration.

s: Which Amendment made the President's assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory?
x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made assent mandatory; the President cannot reject or return such a Bill.

s: Which of the following Bills can the President NOT return for reconsideration?
x: Assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill is mandatory, so it cannot be returned; the one-time return power can apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II.

s: To Financial Bills of which category can the President's one-time power to return a Bill apply?
x: The one-time return power can apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II; Money Bills cannot be returned.

s: How can the veto of the President of the United States be overridden?
x: The US President has a qualified veto, which Congress can override by a two-thirds majority.

s: Which veto does the Indian President have but the US President does not?
x: India has an absolute veto, which the USA lacks; the USA has a qualified veto, which India lacks.

s: Under which Article did the Supreme Court hold in 2025 that a Governor's indefinite inaction on a Bill is justiciable?
x: Indefinite inaction under Article 200 is justiciable, so the Governor has no presidential-style pocket veto.

s: Under which Article does the President declare or withhold assent to a State Bill reserved by the Governor?
x: Article 201 governs reserved State Bills; Article 200 is the Governor's own options.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold about courts in the November 2025 Presidential reference under Article 143?
o: Can fix a three-month timeline for assent
Can declare pending Bills deemed assented
Can direct the President to assent to any Bill
Cannot fix timelines for the Governor or the President
x: The five-judge bench held courts cannot fix timelines and there is no deemed assent, though the powers cannot be used arbitrarily.

s: In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor (8 April 2025), how many Tamil Nadu Bills were deemed assented?
x: The April 2025 ruling held indefinite inaction under Article 200 justiciable and deemed ten TN Bills assented.

s: Which of the following powers does the Governor NOT have over State Bills?
o: Reserving a Bill for the President
x: Under Article 200 the Governor may assent, withhold, return or reserve a Bill, but has no pocket veto.
